idiom_name: typed generator (Generator<T, void, unknown>) as the unfold + a checked accumulator loop as the fold
implementation_notes: The JavaScript realization with the types made explicit: the coalgebra is a function returning Generator<Value, void, unknown> (or IterableIterator<Value>), the algebra is (acc: Acc, v: Value) => Acc, and the fused fold is a for..of loop, so the compiler infers the accumulator type and rejects a mismatched algebra at the call site. Exporting the two halves as separately typed functions keeps the pattern visible - unfold: (seed: S) => Generator<A> and fold: (acc: Acc, a: A) => Acc - and a small generic reduceIter helper restores the combinator form when several folds share one generator. Materialization (Array.from, spread) remains the right call when the sequence is data, and the type system will not warn that the intermediate structure came back.
pitfalls: With a target below ES2015, generators require downlevelIteration and the for..of spread of the generated values behaves differently; check the tsconfig target before promising iterator semantics.
Generator<T> is single-shot exactly as in JavaScript - the type does not make it re-iterable; type the API as Iterable<T> and keep Generator for internal use.
TS 3.6+ requires the TReturn/TNext type arguments (void, unknown) to be explicit in some contexts; letting them infer to any silently erases the element type from the fused fold.
TypeScript cannot see laziness: annotating a helper as returning Iterable<T> hides whether it materializes, so an Array.from sneaked into the unfold chain stays invisible to the compiler.
